body.text: The Interview: Pia Miranda on food, Looking for Alibrandi and the hunt for the Recipe of the Year

It's close to the end of the school day and all you can focus on are the dust motes floating in front of your face — but then your English teacher makes an announcement: today's class will be spent watching Looking for Alibrandi.
And just like that, you're awake.
There aren't many films forced on students that inspire such a response as this 2000 classic.

The widely cherished love letter to food, culture and girlhood in 1990s Sydney is an adaptation of Melina Marchetta's award-winning 1992 novel of the same name, which has itself been widely reported as the "most stolen book" from Australian high school libraries.
Both novel and film explored the inescapable sense of otherness that comes with being anything but Anglo in this country in a way few other texts had at that point.
But Pia Miranda, the film's Italian-Australian lead, is a big part of the enduring allure of the movie adaptation in particular.

Miranda's tender portrayal of the audacious 17-year-old Josie, delightfully unafraid of talking back to her Nonna even on tomato day, earned her a special place in the heart of the nation — as well as the 2000 AACTA Award for best actress in a leading role.
She's been a mainstay on our screens ever since, appearing in everything from The Secret Life of Us, to Invisible Boys, to Australian Survivor.

But throughout Miranda's long and varied career, she's returned to Looking for Alibrandi's bigger themes of food and identity time and again, whether through spots on cooking shows or her 2023 memoir Finding My Bella Vita.

It's perhaps fitting, then, that she will next appear as host of the new cooking series Recipe of the Year, alongside 2010 MasterChef winner and presenter Adam Liaw, as well as Country Women's Association convenor Ellice Schrader.
At the same time, there are whispers of a return to Melina Marchetta's world, this time on the small screen.
So, we caught up with the beloved actor, longtime lover of food and new host for a chat about it all.
As someone who loves food, but who isn't a chef per se, what made you want to host Recipe of the Year?
Almost every day of my life, people come up to me and talk to me about tomato day. So, it makes sense that I'm hosting a cooking show. [Laughs]
And I always wanted to be part of something that [marries] cooking with celebrating multiculturalism in Australia.
Recipe of the Year is really different from most "cooking shows".
We're thinking about real Australia, what being Australian [means] and Australian recipes encapsulate.
And a lot of the time they are recipes that come from our relatives or our backgrounds, which are many and varied.
It's a great time to celebrate different backgrounds and people of diverse heritage in Australia.
This meant a lot to Adam Liaw and I as second-generation Australians.
What was your experience with food growing up in 80s and 90s Melbourne as an Italian-Australian?
Oh gosh, cooking was just such a part of my childhood.
Both sets of my grandparents — on my Italian and Australian side — were fantastic cooks, and I spent a lot of my childhood in the kitchen with them.
That's how we bonded, that's how we celebrated, and that's how I learned to accept and show love.
What about outside your family unit?
Italian food is so accepted and so loved now. But growing up, things like salami were really unusual.
My dad used to make anchovies on white bread for me as a snack after school and I would hide it in the back of my fridge when my friends would come over.
And I remember a rumour went around the school that we had eggplant in our fridge, and people screamed and ran away from me.

Though, to be honest, I was never really embarrassed about it. I remember when the kids were running away from me, I was like, "These kids are absolutely insane because eggplant is delicious" [laughs]. I'm really happy I never shied away from my Italian side.
I think it's really important to remember peoples' experiences of growing up from a migrant background. Being Italian is very celebrated now — it wasn't always.
If we don't revisit those stories, we'll just keep making the same mistakes but with a new group.
Speaking of formative experiences … how did starring in Looking for Alibrandi shape your identity?

What I didn't realise at the time is, 26 years later, I'd still be meeting people in the street who love it. Yesterday, someone brought their Looking for Alibrandi book [to me] and I signed it, and she was so excited and that made her day.
Even on my worst days, I can still meet someone on the street who's so excited to see me and talk about Alibrandi, and that's truly a gift.
Was there ever a point in time when it didn't feel like a gift?
Oh, when I had zero dollars in my bank balance, I wished I'd been paid more [laughs].

It's difficult for a lot of Australian actors, because the financial benefits aren't really there. So, when you lose your anonymity but there's not really any benefits financially, that can be a little tricky to navigate. I think people feel shame around this sort of stuff, but it's really normal to be a successful person working in the arts and not to be financially stable.
But I was always really conscious to never be embittered about it, because I was so lucky to get that role. I've felt lucky everyday, really.
And the experience was so wonderful, my friendship with Melina Marchetta is so important to me. And so, it's truly always felt like a blessing.
What do you think Looking for Alibrandi's legacy is?
Tomato day. [Laughs]

The legacy that has been surprising for me is it's not about Italian-Australians. It speaks to people from all different migrant cultures — people from many varied cultures come up to me and say it meant a lot to them because it's a timeless story of struggling to fit in, of feeling othered, and wanting to conform, but also being a non-conformist.
I think it's a beautiful story and, at the end of the day, she's a feminist icon and we need more of those.
There are reports of a Looking for Alibrandi sequel series in development, to be set 20 years after the original …
There's definitely something around, but it's such early days that I don't know yet.

But I will say this: If I was ever going to revisit such an iconic story, the scripts would have to be incredible and it would still have to be a story that celebrates multiculturalism and migrant stories. That's really important to me.
And I would never do it without Kick Gurry, who played [Josie's love interest] Jacob, in some capacity.
Hard segue back to food! Is there a particular dish you cook for someone when you're trying to show them you really love them?

My Nonna is from a small island off the coast of Sicily, and when she came to Australia, she didn't really have a lot of money. [It's because of her that] I really come into my own when there's not much in the house. I can make something great with some pantry staples.
If you've got flour, some yeast and cheese, you can always make some kind of pizza for someone. And there's something quite ceremonial about making pizza dough.
When you think back to your childhood, is there a particular dish your grandparents made that stands out to you?
There's two that I make for everyone during Christmastime. My Nan used to make lemon slice for everyone, so now I make it and I give it to my cousins and it makes everyone happy.
And my Nonna used to make this Italian gingerbread that you can only really get in the Aeolian Islands, called spicchitedda, and I make that for everyone as well.
The recipe she gave me was word-of-mouth, and she wasn't great with quantities, especially for flavouring.
But over time I've made it, taken it to my dad, and he's said, "Oh, I think maybe you should add a little bit of this", or "I remember Nonna putting this in there".
It's pretty great now. Even my Aussie cousins will text me and be like, "When's the gingerbread happening? It's Christmas!" and they'll come over and get some.
Quotes lightly edited for clarity and brevity.
We've got a story for you. Stream Recipe of the Year on ABC iview or watch on Sundays at 7:30pm from October 11 on ABC TV.
